Hybrid energy storage system

High power and high energy density ESS are both included in the hybrid ESS.The battery forms the high energy density ESS, while the supercapacitor (SC) is the high-power density ESS.To maintain long-term energy balance, the batteries monitor power imbalances in the system caused by variations in renewable generation and load.And by reacting quickly to abrupt power imbalances, the supercapacitor gives the system a degree of inertia and stops significant variations in the system's characteristics (voltage).The battery's operational limits are outlined in Table 2.These limits prevent the battery from being overcharged or excessively discharged, thereby extending its lifespan and maintaining optimal performance.An energy storage system discrete-time model displaying the evolution of stored energy throughout system operation is used here.The dynamic model is derived from the balance equations that describe the State of Charge (SOC) evolution of the batteries during the charge/discharge process, as outlined in 31 :

PV system

In the microgrid setup, photovoltaic panels are integrated with Maximum Power Point Tracking (MPPT) and boost converter technologies, which dynamically optimize energy extraction based on varying irradiation and temperature inputs.The MPPT ensures that the photovoltaic panels operate at their maximum power output by continuously adjusting the operating point to match the varying environmental conditions.Additionally, the boost converter efficiently increases the voltage of the photovoltaic output to match the requirements of the microgrid.The photovoltaic panel array comprises 22 modules connected in parallel and 8 in series, with each module having a capacity of 305 watts, yielding a total of 53 kilowatts.The equations define the diode I-V characteristics for a single module 32 :

Load

In this microgrid configuration, the load is intricately managed.The load's model is specifically designed to handle both active power (P) and reactive power (Q), ensuring comprehensive control over power consumption.Moreover, this load is dynamically regulated by Model Predictive Control (MPC), allowing for precise and adaptive management of power consumption based on real-time grid conditions and operational requirements.

If the load's terminal voltage V is less than a predetermined value V min , the load impedance is maintained constant.The active power P and reactive power Q of the load change in the following ways when the terminal voltage is higher than the V min value 33 :
P (s) = P0 ( V V0 ) np 1 + Tp1 1 + Tp2 (4) Q (s) = Q0 ( V V0 ) nq 1 + Tq1 1 + Tq2 (5)

where V 0 is the initial positive sequence voltage, P 0 and Q 0 are the initial active and reactive powers at the initial voltage V 0 , V is the positive-sequence voltage, n p and n q are exponents (usually between 1 and 3) controlling the nature of the load, T p1 and T p2 are time constants controlling the dynamics of the active power P, and T q1 and T q2 are time constants controlling the dynamics of the reactive power Q.
Model predictive controller for demand side management

The problem description and control goals within the MPC formulation are presented in this section.The suggested energy management model must implement Demand Side Management (DSM) strategies that benefit the utility, including load curtailment and load shifting.These strategies are essential for balancing supply and demand, especially during peak usage periods.This involves anticipating future energy requirements and dynamically adjusting the power distribution to optimize the use of available resources.By incorporating DSM strategies, the model not only improves the utility's operational efficiency but also enhances the resilience of the microgrid.Figure 2 shows the simulation scheme of the control architecture presented here using Matlab.
Control objective

The suggested MPC plan basically seeks to achieve the following goals: 1) Increase the prosumer's revenue by utilizing batteries and Renewable Energy Sources more frequently.2) Reduce demand by curtailing and shifting loads at predetermined intervals.3) Prevent ESS against significant fluctuations in the SOC by avoiding deep and overcharging.Due to several microgrid operational constraints, some above cited objectives may be conflicting, and other ones are complementary.Thus, to encompass such objectives while achieving the optimal allocation of energy resources, the MPC strategy aims mainly to manage sudden changes in energy supply and rapid variations in demand.
Control architecture

Figure 2 illustrates the integration of the microgrid, the model predictive control (MPC), and the artificial neural network (ANN) block.In this configuration, the MPC uses the state of charge of the hybrid energy storage system (SOC batt ) and (SOC sc ) as inputs and generates reference values for the manipulated variables: grid power (P grid ), battery power (P batt ), and load power (P load ).These reference values are then passed to the microgrid.Simultaneously, the ANN block processes inputs such as irradiation (GHI and GTI) and temperature (T) to predict the output of the PV panel (P pred ) 34 .The predicted PV panel values are subsequently fed into the MPC as measured disturbances, enabling dynamic system optimization.Consequently, during operation, the MPC controller also maintains the desired outputs around a certain level of stored energy, corresponding to the reference values for the states of charge of the hybrid energy storage system [SOCref batt , SOCref sc ], thus Fig. 2. Microgrid linear model

Obtaining a linear model of the system to be controlled around a working point (x * ,y * ) is necessary for the use of linear MPC techniques.Nowadays, state space representation is the standard method for modeling when implementing MPC strategies 30,31 .The following state space description of a linear time-invariant system is discussed:
x (k + 1) = Ax (k) + Bu (k) + B d d (k)(6)

Moreover, the model includes an additional variable related to the power of the Supercapacitor P SC (k), which is not directly controlled from the MPC as it must compensate for the total power.Its control occurs indirectly through a balance equation that manages the energy excess or deficit at the DC bus.It adjusts quickly to power imbalances, absorbing or providing energy as needed.By reacting rapidly to fluctuations in power, the supercapacitor stabilizes the system, offering a level of inertia and preventing significant voltage variations that could destabilize the grid.The equation fulfilling the energy balance in the DC bus can be expressed as:
P batt (k) + P sc (k) + P grid (k) + P gen (k) − P load (k) = 0 (10)   These results are obtained by minimizing cost function J, as will be discussed in the following section.
Cost function formulations

Ensuring a steady supply of electricity to its residents is EMS's main objective.These goals' accomplishment can be linked to their weights in the cost function.This cost function weighs the use of the manipulated variable, penalizes the rate, and helps maintain the stored energy near an operating point:

The forecast-based scheduling in MPC helps reduce battery degradation, particularly calendar aging.By using forecasts, MPC can access information about future generation, enabling it to adjust the battery charge-discharge cycle.This prevents the battery from remaining in a charged state for extended periods, thus reducing calendar aging.It is important to note that the explicit use of the battery degradation equation was not considered here due to its non-linear nature, which can lead to more complex and computationally intensive optimization problems 35 .To avoid this, the cost function is maintained as quadratic, as shown in Eq. ( 11), resulting in a quadratic programming problem that can be solved efficiently 36 .Table 1 outlines the weight values assigned to each group in this work, which were derived empirically through extensive computational testing.The selection of these weights establishes the priority among the objectives.The weighting factors were determined using a trial-and-error approach, guided by the MATLAB MPC design rules.This method ensures that the selected values achieve a balanced trade-off between competing objectives while preserving system stability and performance.
Operational constraints

A microgrid is made up of various parts, each of which has specific constraints that must be considered while operating.A careful value for SOC batt and SOC SC limits the energy storage system's working range.The producers claim that making this assumption prevents overcharging and undercharging, which significantly shorten the batteries' usable lives.The minimum load constraint accounts for the operation of devices that must always remain on, such as refrigerators and freezers.These constraints are given in Table 2 below:

Linear modeling is used in this case because the system dynamics and constraints are linear, which simplifies the problem and ensures computational efficiency.Although the objective function is quadratic (11), it is still suitable for linear MPC, as quadratic cost functions are convex and can be optimized effectively within a linear framework.Additionally, MPC is well-suited for these scenarios because it allows for predictive control while handling constraints systematically, providing an optimal control strategy even with a quadratic objective function 31 .
Simulations results and discussions

A full model was developed that incorporates all the schematic elements-load, photovoltaics, grid energy, and hybrid energy storage-that are described in Section I.The internal plant model is represented by the state space representation in Eq. ( 9), whereas the controller used is the MPC explained in section II.The results are obtained using the cost function from Eq. ( 11) along with the constraints given in Table 2 and the weights for the cost function listed in Table 1.

Building on this configuration, the model is extended to assess the accuracy of disturbance predictions across four scenarios: real-time, and one, two, or three hours ahead of the real-time operation, considering two different weather conditions.This approach enables an assessment of the model's responsiveness and effectiveness in anticipating external changes that affect operational efficiency.

The weight values in Table 1 for the SOC of the lithium-ion batteries give freedom for charge/discharge operations allowing to store most of the photovoltaic power and almost reaching lithium-ion batteries operational constraints given by SOCli,max limit.In this setup, the photovoltaic panel has a capacity of 53 kW, while the battery can store up to a maximum of 108 kWh.

Considering the energy output from the photovoltaic panel and the battery's capacity, the timing of battery discharging and charging is selected.The optimal case called scenario 1 is to use forecasts made one hour in advance, the battery synchronizes its charging and discharging based on the current ability of the PV generation.This implies that the battery adjusts its operations in real-time to match the availability of power from the photovoltaic panels.Conversely, in the no-delay scenario 4 where predictions are made instantaneously or very close to real-time, the battery tends to charge less, and discharge more compared to the reference case.This delay in anticipating the available power from the photovoltaic panels causes the battery to miss opportunities for optimal charging, the battery's charging is postponed, making it dependent on the grid at the end of the charging period.Figures 3 and 4 display the battery flow for each scenario in comparison to the power flow of the PV panel on sunny and cloudy days, respectively.On the other hand, when predictions are made two or three hours in advance (scenario 2 and 3 respectively), the battery adjusts its strategy to anticipate future conditions.It tends to discharge less and charge more in preparation for expected solar power over the longer forecasting horizon.However, this proactive approach can lead to the need for the load to purchase more energy from the grid to compensate for any shortfall that the battery cannot cover, resulting in inefficient use of its capacity.

To evaluate the impact of implementing a DRP during the day, two approaches are considered: shifting and curtailment.The study highlights how load-shifting strategies can work alongside curtailment to improve grid stability.Two load-shifting cases are examined.In case 1, load curtailment is scheduled for the morning (6 to 8 AM) and afternoon (4 to 6 PM), while case 2 has load curtailment from 10 AM to 1 PM, with curtailment implemented at varying times depending on the specific shifting process in each case.For each scenario, a 24-h simulation period was conducted under two different generation conditions-sunny and cloudy-to assess the effectiveness of the control system on the proposed micro-grid.It's essential to recognize that the decrease in electricity consumption takes place during the pre-defined hours through load curtailments, thereby minimizing the reliance on the main grid during these times.

In the early morning hours before sunrise, the battery supplies power to the load, supplemented by energy from the grid if necessary.As the sun rises, the photovoltaic system takes over to meet the load requirements, recharge the battery, and export surplus energy to the grid.In Fig. 5, load curtailment occurring in the morning and afternoon, resulting in a high load during midday.The grid balances the gap between the load and photovoltaic power, and the supercapacitor compensates for any variations.However, in Fig. 6, load curtailment happens around noon, resulting in making the grid follow the photovoltaic curve while taking advantage of the midday peak.Consequently, the supercapacitor has to compensate significantly more compared to Case 1.This implies that implementing a 3-h curtailment during midday proves to be less benefit comparable to  implementing a 4-h curtailment in the morning and afternoon, especially on sunny days, as the supercapacitor has to compensate more.

Furthermore, since more energy needs to be imported from the grid during cloudy periods in Figs.7 and  8, emphasizing the priority placed on exporting surplus energy.On the other hand, the microgrid system's stability and resilience depend on the supercapacitor's quick response to shifting energy dynamics.As a result, the batteries responsible for satisfying the required demand do not perceive sudden fluctuations.The MPC controller has demonstrated satisfactory performance in all scenarios, effectively maintaining the energy balance at many operational points throughout the day.These findings demonstrate that, even in extreme circumstances, the MPC controller functions to fulfill the predetermined goals specified by the cost function, just as it is intended to.

Table 3 provides a summary of fuel prices for a city near Berlin across six daily periods.It highlights incentive mechanism like Time-of-Use Pricing, aimed at promoting user participation in demand response initiatives by facilitating energy usage shifts or curtailments when needed.The price of buying energy from the grid is low during midday peak hours because renewable energy sources, like solar, are generating more power, reducing the need for grid supply.However, in the early morning or afternoon, when renewable generation is lower, the grid must supply more power, leading to higher prices for purchasing energy.Meanwhile, selling energy to the grid is more valuable during midday, when demand is high, leading to higher prices for selling and lower prices at other times.Additionally, Table 4 shows the cost of electricity as well as the power purchased and sold from and to the grid.Table 5shows a comparison of several control strategies.Where, only one approach 18 , showed higher energy savings by over 4%, but this method does not account for energy storage.

It is clear from Table 4, that in case 2 the model is purchasing more from the grid and simultaneously selling more, the overall balance shows that case 2 is buying more than it is selling when compared to case 1 for the same amount of load due to restrictions during peak solar periods, missing optimal generation opportunities.This forces the grid to adjust to photovoltaic irradiation fluctuations, increasing the supercapacitor's workload.Conversely, Case 1 manages curtailment effectively during less critical times, optimizing energy usage and generation.The supercapacitor regulates the gap between PV power and load, leading to more stable and predictable operation with reduced strain.Similar outcomes are observed under cloudy conditions, albeit with a slightly smaller difference.

Furthermore the results indicate that load shifting can reduce grid energy usage and associated costs by up to 48%, accounting for the balance between energy purchased from and sold to the grid.On cloudy days, the reduction is up to 34%, which can be attributed to the lack of PV power, leading to greater reliance on the grid.08:00-10:00 €0.12 €0.14 10:00-14:00 €0.15 €0.12 14:00-18:00 €0.13 €0.14 18:00-24:00 €0.09 €0.17

Conclusion

This   18 and 19 utilize EMPC as the control method.When disturbances and demand-side management areimplemented, energy consumption can be reduced by 52%; however, this is achieved without incorporating any storage system.Furthermore, when AMPC is used, as in 13 and 15 , the operation cost of the system can be reduced by 29.4% while adding disturbances, and by 46% when both demand response and disturbances are incorporated.And since disturbances cannot be incorporated into the system with the fuzzy logic controller 41 , Golden Jackal Optimization method 42 , Differential Evolution (DE) 38 and heuristic-based optimization algorithm 40 , the emphasis is placed solely on load-shifting demand response, resulting in a 33.72%, 26% and 10-13% reduction in electricity costs, and a 15% reduction in grid consumption, respectively 17,39 ., and 11  supercapacitor, which is vital for maintaining grid stability during sudden fluctuations, thereby enhancing the efficiency of the hybrid energy storage system.This approach lowers grid energy usage and costs by up to 48% on sunny days and 34% on cloudy days, accounting for energy trade with the grid.Overall, the findings underscore the significance of optimizing energy management systems within microgrids to maximize renewable energy usage, especially under varying weather conditions.The innovative application of the proposed methods suggests considerable potential for future research, particularly in refining predictive models that consider real-time solar generation and load changes.Future investigations should also focus on assessing the performance of MPC amid forecast uncertainties.
